  age: 28
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Media / News: Related news, Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened, Children Present: Being around children
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Vignette:
Liam, a 28-year-old financial analyst, vividly remembers the day everything changed. It was a cold, driving rain outside, the kind that made the world feel grey and muffled, when his son, Leo, then just a toddler, developed a sudden, alarming fever. The memory is a series of sharp, almost photographic images: Leo’s small body convulsing, his lips tinged blue, the frantic rush to the emergency room, the blinding fluorescent lights of the hospital, and the sound of machines beeping around his son's crib. He recalls the feeling of absolute powerlessness, a visceral conviction that he should have been able to protect his child, a failure that still gnaws at him.

Even now, months later, those images are startlingly clear, replaying in his mind with painful detail, especially the visual memories of Leo’s pale face and the tubes connected to his tiny arm. Yet, he often finds himself pushing the memory away before he can fully recall the most frightening moments, as if his mind is trying to shield him from the full force of the terror.

The world outside has become a minefield of reminders. A news report about a child’s rare illness, a segment on medical breakthroughs, or even a general health crisis can send a jolt of panic through him, making him feel as if he is back in that sterile hospital room. The weather itself can be a trigger; a cold, rainy day like the one Leo fell ill immediately plunges him into a state of hyper-alertness, his heart racing as if danger is imminent. What frightens him most, though, is being around other children. A child’s cry in a supermarket, a group of kids laughing in the park, or even the sight of Leo playing boisterously, can bring the fear flooding back, a stark reminder of how fragile life can be.

This constant state of readiness has seeped into every corner of Liam’s life. He often reacts as if he is in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, a sudden noise or an unexpected movement making him jump. He finds himself constantly scanning his surroundings, whether in the busy trading floor of his office or a quiet restaurant with his wife, always identifying potential escape routes before he can feel comfortable anywhere. He might choose a seat near an exit, or mentally map out the quickest way to the stairwell. At night, sleep offers little reprieve. He has difficulty falling asleep because he feels an overwhelming need to stay alert, listening for any sound from Leo’s room, despite his son being healthy now. He lies awake, his senses on high alert, convinced that something terrible could happen if he lets his guard down.

Liam looks at himself in the mirror and often feels like he doesn't know the person staring back. The easygoing, confident man he was before Leo’s illness feels distant, replaced by someone perpetually on edge, constantly vigilant. He has come to believe that the person he has become is unrecognisable to him, and at times, to his wife too. He carries a profound sense of guilt, the persistent thought that he should have protected his son better, and that he failed in his most fundamental role as a father. This belief colors his interactions, making him withdraw, at times, from the very people he loves.

The changes have accumulated over weeks and months. His focus at work, once sharp and unwavering, is now frequently interrupted by intrusive thoughts or sudden bursts of anxiety. He finds himself distracted during important client calls, his mind drifting to potential threats instead of market trends. His wife has noticed his withdrawal, the way he avoids social gatherings where other children might be present, or how he seems distant even when they are together. Liam knows he needs help. He finally sought therapy after a particularly jarring panic attack in his office, triggered by a news headline about a local hospital, leaving him shaken and certain that he couldn't continue living this way. He desperately wants to feel like himself again, to shed the constant fear, but he is terrified that this new, hyper-vigilant version of himself is permanent.
